specStatements.text: Momentum is defined by the equation:
momentum, p, in kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
This is called conservation of momentum.
Students should be able to use the concept of momentum as a model to:
• describe and explain examples of momentum in a n event, such as a collision
• (physics only) complete calculations involving an event, such as the collision of two objects.
When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs.
The equations F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
combine to give the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)
where m ∆ v = change in momentum
ie force equals the rate of change of momentum.

Students should be able to explain safety features such as: air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned surfaces for playgrounds with reference to the concept of rate of change of momentum.
Students should be able to apply equations relating force, mass, velocity and acceleration to explain how the changes involved are inter-related.

scopeNotes.statement: • (physics only) complete calculations involving an event, such as the collision of two objects.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification limits the calculation of an event to the separate GCSE Physics course. Combined Science students are required only to describe and explain examples of momentum in an event. Every calculation item here (q14, q15, q16) is therefore marked 'physics only' in its stem, and none of it is treated as a prerequisite for the qualitative work in 4.5.7.2, which is carried by items needing no arithmetic (c09, c10, m08, m10, q10, q12, q13). The calculations themselves stay inside the specification's own example: an event such as the collision of two objects, along a single line, in a closed system. No two-dimensional momentum, no vector diagrams and no algebraic treatment of a general collision are introduced.

The whole of 4.5.7 is Higher Tier only, so every concept, misconception and question here is tagged tier 'higher' and none of it is offered as Foundation content or assumed of a Foundation student. The material also respects the boundary in the other direction: the word 'impulse' is never used, because the specification does not name it; collisions are never classified as elastic or inelastic using kinetic energy, because the specification does not ask for that; and momentum is treated only along a single line with one direction taken as positive, which is all the specification's own example of a collision of two objects requires.

The specification heading for 4.5.7.3 reads 'Changes in momentum (physics only)', so the whole sub-section sits outside the Combined Science route. Combined Science students meet momentum only through 4.5.7.1 and the qualitative half of 4.5.7.2; F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), rate of change of momentum and the safety-feature explanations are not theirs. Every item on 4.5.7.3 is therefore marked: statements S12-S18 and concepts c11-c17 all point here, misconceptions m13-m16, m20 and m21 are carried only by those statements, and questions q17-q24 are prefixed '(physics only)' in the stem exactly as the calculation items q14-q16 are. Nothing on 4.5.7.3 is treated as a prerequisite for the 4.5.7.1 and 4.5.7.2 material that Combined Science students do sit.

concepts.definition: A property of a moving object, defined by the specification as an equation: momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving, however large its mass is.
The word equation that defines momentum. It is one of the equations students must recall, so it has to be learned rather than looked up, and both quantities must be in SI units before it is used.
The symbol form of the definition: p stands for momentum, m for mass and v for velocity. Writing the symbols out before substituting keeps momentum separate from F = m × a, which shares the symbol m.
The unit of momentum. It is a compound unit built from the units of the two quantities being multiplied: kilograms for mass and metres per second for velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.
In p = m v the mass, m, must be in kilograms. A mass quoted in grams or tonnes has to be converted first: divide grams by 1000, multiply tonnes by 1000.
In p = m v the velocity, v, must be in metres per second. A speed quoted in km/h is converted by dividing by 3.6. Velocity also has a direction, so momentum has a direction too.

A system in which no mass enters or leaves and no external resultant force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, and it is that condition which makes the total momentum before and after an event equal.

The name given to the statement that, in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after the event. It applies to the total for the whole system, not to each object separately.

Anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving: a collision, objects sticking together, or an explosion pushing objects apart. Momentum is used as a model to describe and explain what happens in such an event.

An event in which objects initially at rest push each other apart. The total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum after must also be zero: the two objects move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size.
Newton's second law: the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration. It is one of the two equations the specification combines to obtain the momentum form of the law.
The acceleration equation: acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken. Substituting it into F = m × a is what produces the momentum form of the second law.
The quantity m ∆ v, the mass multiplied by the change in velocity. Because momentum is m v, multiplying the same mass by the change in velocity gives the change in momentum, in kg m/s.
The equation formed by combining F = m × a with a = (v - u)/(t). The force equals the change in momentum divided by the time over which that change happens.

How quickly momentum changes, that is the change in momentum divided by the time taken. The specification states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, so the same change spread over a longer time means a smaller force.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, the object's momentum changes. The force changes the velocity, and since momentum is mass × velocity with the mass fixed, the momentum must change with it.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned playground surfaces. Each one increases the time taken for the change in momentum to happen, which reduces the rate of change of momentum and so reduces the force.

misconceptions.question: A bullet moves far faster than a lorry. Must the bullet have the greater momentum?
misconceptions.correct: No. Momentum is mass × velocity, and the lorry's very large mass more than compensates for its low speed.
misconceptions.misconception: Whatever is moving fastest must have the most momentum, because momentum is really about speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'momentum' means something like unstoppable speed, and the first examples students meet vary the speed while leaving mass unmentioned.
misconceptions.correction: Calculate both. Multiply mass by velocity for each object and compare the two numbers.

misconceptions.question: An 8000 kg lorry crawls at 2 m/s; a 1000 kg car does 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?
misconceptions.correct: The car: 1000 × 20 = 20 000 kg m/s, against 8000 × 2 = 16 000 kg m/s for the lorry.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier object always has the greater momentum, because momentum is about how massive something is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the first quantity in the equation and the most striking feature of a lorry, so students compare masses and stop before finishing the multiplication.
misconceptions.correction: Neither quantity decides alone. Work out mass × velocity for both objects before comparing.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of momentum?
misconceptions.correct: Kilograms metre per second, kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is measured in newtons, or in newtons per second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Momentum is first met alongside forces and crashes, and students associate the push of a collision with the newton.
misconceptions.correction: Build the unit from the equation: kg for mass multiplied by m/s for velocity gives kg m/s.

misconceptions.question: Is kg m/s² an acceptable way to write the unit of momentum?
misconceptions.correct: No. kg m/s² is the newton, the unit of force; momentum is in kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The unit of momentum has a squared second in it, like the unit of acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry the s² across from acceleration and from F = m × a, where kg m/s² really is the correct combination.
misconceptions.correction: Only the units of the quantities in the equation appear: momentum is mass × velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.

misconceptions.question: A ball has a mass of 400 g and moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
misconceptions.correct: 2 kg m/s, because 400 g must first be converted to 0.4 kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is 2000 kg m/s: substitute the mass as it is given, 400 × 5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question looks ready to use, and the unit kg m/s is not read as an instruction about the mass.
misconceptions.correction: Convert to SI units before substituting: divide a mass in grams by 1000 to get kilograms.

misconceptions.question: A car travels at 72 km/h. Can that number be used directly in p = m v?
misconceptions.correct: No. The velocity must be converted to metres per second first: 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Any speed can be substituted into p = m v as it is quoted, whatever unit it is in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: km/h is the unit students see on road signs and in car adverts, so it feels like the natural unit of speed.
misconceptions.correction: Check the unit of every quantity first. Velocity must be in m/s, so divide a speed in km/h by 3.6.

misconceptions.question: Two trolleys of equal mass approach each other at the same speed. What is the total momentum?
misconceptions.correct: Zero, because they move in opposite directions, so their momenta have opposite signs and cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: The total is found by adding the two momenta as plain numbers, giving double the momentum of one trolley.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Momentum is introduced through a multiplication, so it is treated like mass or energy, a quantity with size but no direction.
misconceptions.correction: Choose one direction as positive and give any momentum in the other direction a negative sign before adding.

misconceptions.question: A moving trolley hits a stationary one and slows down. Has momentum been conserved?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The momentum lost by the first trolley has been gained by the second, so the total is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Conservation of momentum means every object keeps the momentum it started with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'conserved' suggests nothing changes anywhere, so it is applied to each object instead of to the system total.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation applies to the total for the closed system: add up all the momenta before and after and compare those totals.

misconceptions.question: A car crashes into a wall and stops. Where has its momentum gone?
misconceptions.correct: To the wall and the Earth it is attached to; the system is only closed if they are included.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is simply destroyed in a crash, which is why the car ends up with none.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The car visibly stops and nothing else appears to move, so momentum seems to vanish rather than transfer.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the whole closed system first. Momentum is transferred to whatever exerted the force, even if that object is far too massive for its motion to be seen.

misconceptions.question: Two skaters at rest push apart. What is the total momentum after the push?
misconceptions.correct: Zero, the same as before: the skaters have equal and opposite momenta.
misconceptions.misconception: They are both moving afterwards, so the system must have gained momentum from the push.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Motion is equated with momentum, and the direction of the two velocities is not taken into account.
misconceptions.correction: Before the push the total is zero, so the total afterwards is also zero: the two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.

misconceptions.question: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg trolley at rest and they stick together. What mass is moving afterwards?
misconceptions.correct: 3 kg, the combined mass of the two trolleys.
misconceptions.misconception: The moving mass afterwards is still 2 kg, because that is the trolley that was moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first trolley is the one 'doing' the moving, so the second is treated as being carried along rather than as part of the mass.
misconceptions.correction: When objects stick together they move as one object: add the masses before dividing the total momentum by them.

misconceptions.question: Is momentum the same thing as kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Momentum is m v; kinetic energy is a different quantity, calculated differently.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is worked out with a half and a squared velocity, like ½ m v².
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities involve mass and speed and are met in the same topic, so the two formulae become blurred.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum uses velocity once, with no half and no square: p = m v, in kg m/s.

misconceptions.question: An air bag inflates in a crash. What does it change?
misconceptions.correct: The time taken for the passenger's momentum to fall to zero, which is made longer.
misconceptions.misconception: The air bag reduces the passenger's change in momentum, so there is less momentum to get rid of.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reducing the impact' is heard as reducing everything about it, and the change in momentum is confused with the force.
misconceptions.correction: The change in momentum is fixed by the mass and the change in velocity. The safety feature lengthens the time, which lowers the rate of change of momentum and so the force.

misconceptions.question: How does a seat belt reduce the force on a passenger?
misconceptions.correct: By stretching slightly, so the passenger is brought to rest over a longer time.
misconceptions.misconception: A seat belt works by stopping the passenger more quickly, before they can hit anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Seat belts are described as holding you firmly in place, which sounds like stopping you sooner rather than later.
misconceptions.correction: A shorter stopping time gives a larger rate of change of momentum and a larger force. The belt must extend the time, not cut it.

misconceptions.question: A gymnast lands on a crash mat instead of the bare floor. Why is the force smaller?
misconceptions.correct: The mat squashes, so the gymnast's momentum changes over a longer time.
misconceptions.misconception: The crash mat absorbs the force, so less of the force reaches the gymnast.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Absorbing the impact' is an everyday phrase, and force is imagined as a substance that can be soaked up.
misconceptions.correction: Force is not a stored substance. The mat increases the time for the same change in momentum, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.

misconceptions.question: In F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what happens to the force if the time is longer?
misconceptions.correct: The force is smaller, because the same change in momentum is divided by a bigger time.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer time gives a bigger force, because the force has longer to act.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the equation as a product rather than a quotient, and 'more time' is assumed to mean 'more of everything'.
misconceptions.correction: ∆t is on the bottom of the fraction, so increasing it decreases the force.

misconceptions.question: Which equation defines momentum: p = m v or p = m a?
misconceptions.correct: p = m v. Momentum is mass × velocity; mass × acceleration gives force.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum equals mass multiplied by acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both equations begin with mass and are taught within days of each other, so the second quantity is mixed up.
misconceptions.correction: Check what the second quantity is: velocity gives momentum in kg m/s, acceleration gives force in newtons.

misconceptions.question: Should the weight of a car be used in p = m v?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation needs the mass in kilograms, not the weight in newtons.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are the same 'how heavy' quantity, so either can be substituted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday use 'weight' is quoted in kilograms, which hides the distinction the physics makes.
misconceptions.correction: Weight is a force in newtons; mass is in kilograms. Only the mass belongs in p = m v.

misconceptions.question: Does a closed system mean a system with a lid on it, or one in which nothing moves?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. It means no mass enters or leaves and no external resultant force acts.
misconceptions.misconception: A closed system is a sealed container, or a system in which nothing is moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'closed' is a shut box, so the condition is read as a physical enclosure rather than as a condition on mass and force.
misconceptions.correction: Ask instead whether anything outside the chosen objects is pushing on them or adding mass to them.

misconceptions.question: Is the rate of change of momentum the same as the change of momentum?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate is the change divided by the time over which it happens.
misconceptions.misconception: Force equals the change in momentum, and the time makes no difference to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Rate of change' is a compound phrase and the 'rate of' part is dropped, especially as both are described in terms of the same crash.
misconceptions.correction: 'Rate of' always means 'per second'. A change of 300 kg m/s in 0.1 s is a force of 3000 N; the same change in 1 s is 300 N.

misconceptions.question: A trolley's momentum changes from 12 kg m/s to 4 kg m/s. What is the change in momentum?
misconceptions.correct: A decrease of 8 kg m/s: final minus initial, 4 - 12 = -8 kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The change is 16 kg m/s, found by adding the two momenta together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students add the numbers in the question rather than subtracting, especially when both are described as momenta of the same trolley.
misconceptions.correction: Change means final value minus initial value: subtract, and take the direction into account if the object rebounds.

misconceptions.question: A trolley of mass 5 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. Do you multiply or divide to find its velocity?
misconceptions.correct: Divide: v = p / m = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Whatever the question asks for, the two numbers given should be multiplied, because p = m v is a multiplication.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is met as a multiplication and is practised that way, so the operation is remembered rather than the rearrangement.
misconceptions.correction: Decide which symbol is unknown first, rearrange p = m v for that symbol, and only then substitute.

misconceptions.question: In a collision the total momentum is 12 kg m/s and the moving mass afterwards is 5 kg. What is the velocity?
misconceptions.correct: 2.4 m/s: the total momentum must still be divided by the mass that is moving.
misconceptions.misconception: The total momentum is the answer, so the velocity after the collision is 12.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of momentum gives a number that feels like the final answer, and the last step of dividing by the mass is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation gives the momentum after the event, not the velocity. Divide that momentum by the mass that is moving.

misconceptions.question: A skater at rest pushes a sledge away. Do the skater and the sledge move at the same speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their momenta are equal in size, so the heavier one moves more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: They must move apart at the same speed, since each one pushed the other equally hard.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Newton's third law gives equal forces, and equal forces are assumed to produce equal speeds whatever the masses are.
misconceptions.correction: Set the two momenta equal: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂. The larger mass then has the smaller velocity.

mcqs.stem: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?

options.text: momentum = mass × acceleration
options.rationale: Chosen by students who blend p = m v with F = m × a; both equations open with mass and are taught within days of each other.

options.text: momentum = weight × velocity
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat weight and mass as the same 'how heavy' quantity.

options.text: momentum = mass × velocity
options.rationale: This is the defining word equation given in 4.5.7.1, and it is one of the equations students are required to recall.

options.text: momentum = force × velocity
options.rationale: Selected by students who link momentum to the force felt in an impact rather than to the mass of the object.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol equation for momentum does the specification give?

options.text: p = m × a
options.rationale: The mass × acceleration combination, which gives force, not momentum.

options.text: p = ½ m v²
options.rationale: The kinetic energy expression, chosen by students who merge two quantities that both involve mass and speed.

options.text: p = m v²
options.rationale: A half-remembered energy form; momentum uses the velocity once, not squared.

options.text: p = m v
options.rationale: The symbol form printed in 4.5.7.1: p for momentum, m for mass, v for velocity.

mcqs.stem: Which unit does the specification give for momentum, p?

options.text: kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
options.rationale: The unit printed in 4.5.7.1, and the one built by multiplying kg by m/s.

options.text: kilogram per metre second, kg/m s
options.rationale: Formed by dividing rather than multiplying, so mass and velocity are combined the wrong way round.

options.text: newtons per second squared, N/s²
options.rationale: Chosen by students who associate momentum with the push of a collision, so reach for the newton.

options.text: newton metres per second, N m/s
options.rationale: Another newton-based guess; the newton belongs to force, and no force appears in p = m v.

mcqs.stem: A ball has a mass of 400 g and travels at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.text: 2 kg m/s
80 kg m/s
options.rationale: Obtained by dividing 400 by 5 instead of multiplying, and leaving the mass in grams.

options.text: 0.4 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass converted correctly to kilograms, but the multiplication by the velocity never carried out.

options.text: 2000 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass substituted in grams: 400 × 5. The unit kg m/s is a reminder that mass must be in kilograms.

mcqs.stem: A lorry's speed is given as 54 km/h. What must be done before this value is used in p = m v?

options.text: It must be converted to metres per second, by dividing by 3.6, because v in p = m v is in m/s
options.rationale: The specification gives velocity, v, in metres per second, so a speed in km/h has to be converted first.

options.text: It must be converted to metres per hour, by multiplying the number of kilometres by 1000
options.rationale: A half-done conversion: the distance unit is fixed but the time unit is left in hours.

options.text: It can be substituted just as it is, provided the mass of the lorry is given in kilograms
options.rationale: Chosen by students who check only the mass, since km/h is the unit of speed they meet daily.

options.text: It must be multiplied by 3.6, the number that converts between the two units of speed
options.rationale: The right conversion factor used the wrong way round, which makes the speed larger rather than smaller.

mcqs.stem: A skateboarder of mass 60 kg moves at 4 m/s. What is the skateboarder's momentum?

options.text: 15 kg m/s
options.rationale: Found by dividing 60 by 4; the defining equation is a multiplication.

options.text: 0.067 kg m/s
options.rationale: Found by dividing 4 by 60, so mass and velocity have been used the wrong way round.

options.text: 240 kg m/s

options.rationale: The right number given the unit of force, which is what students reach for when momentum is met through collisions.

mcqs.stem: A 40 000 kg lorry moves at 3 m/s. A 1200 kg car moves at 30 m/s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The car has the greater momentum, because it is the faster moving of the two vehicles
options.rationale: Speed alone is compared, which is how the word 'momentum' is used in everyday speech.

options.text: They have equal momentum, since the lorry's extra mass is cancelled by the car's extra speed
options.rationale: An appealing symmetry, but the numbers do not balance: 120 000 against 36 000.

options.text: The lorry has the greater momentum: 120 000 kg m/s against only 36 000 kg m/s for the car
options.rationale: 40 000 × 3 = 120 000 kg m/s and 1200 × 30 = 36 000 kg m/s, so the lorry's momentum is larger.

options.text: The lorry has the greater momentum, because momentum simply depends on a vehicle's mass
options.rationale: The right vehicle for the wrong reason: masses are compared without completing the multiplication.

mcqs.stem: A trolley of mass 5 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. What is its velocity?

options.text: 60 m/s
options.rationale: Found by multiplying 12 by 5; the equation must be rearranged before substituting.
Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.
Found by dividing 5 by 12, so the rearrangement has been made upside down.

options.text: 2.4 kg m/s
options.rationale: The right number carrying the unit of momentum instead of the unit of velocity.

mcqs.stem: Why is the unit of momentum kilograms metre per second?

options.text: Because it is the unit of force multiplied by the unit of the time for which that force acts
options.rationale: A statement that sounds mechanical and plausible, but it is not how the specification builds the unit.

options.text: Because momentum is mass × acceleration, so the unit is kg multiplied by m/s² instead
options.rationale: Uses acceleration in place of velocity, which is the combination that gives the newton.

options.text: Because momentum is a compound quantity, so its unit is always a compound unit too
options.rationale: True of the form of the unit but not an explanation: it says nothing about which quantities are used.

options.text: Because momentum is mass × velocity, so the unit must be kg multiplied by m/s, or kg m/s
options.rationale: The unit of any quantity comes from the equation defining it: kg × m/s = kg m/s.

mcqs.stem: The specification states conservation of momentum for a closed system. What is a closed system?

options.text: One in which the objects are all sealed inside a container, so that nothing can escape from it
options.rationale: The everyday sense of 'closed' as a shut box, rather than a condition on mass and force.

options.text: One in which no mass enters or leaves and no resultant force acts on it from outside the system
options.rationale: This is the condition under which the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.

options.text: One in which nothing is moving, so that the total momentum of the system stays equal to zero
options.rationale: Confuses a closed system with a stationary one; closed systems very often contain moving objects.

options.text: One in which the objects touch each other, so that momentum can be passed from one to another
options.rationale: Contact matters during a collision, but it is not what makes a system closed.

mcqs.stem: In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. What is this called?

options.text: Newton's third law of motion
options.rationale: Related to collisions, but it is a statement about pairs of forces, not about a total before and after.

options.text: Conservation of net force
options.rationale: Force is not a conserved quantity, and the statement is about momentum, not force.

options.text: Conservation of momentum
options.rationale: This is the name the specification gives to the statement in 4.5.7.2.

options.text: Conservation of energy
options.rationale: Chosen by students who blur momentum and kinetic energy; energy conservation is a different statement.

mcqs.stem: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. Which statement about their momentum is correct?

options.text: They have equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero, as it was before the push
options.rationale: The total momentum before the push is zero, and in a closed system the total after must also be zero.

options.text: Both of the skaters are now moving, so the system has gained momentum from the push they gave
options.rationale: Motion is equated with momentum and the opposite directions are not taken into account.

options.text: Momentum is not conserved here, because the skaters were not moving before they pushed
options.rationale: A total of zero is still a total: conservation applies to systems that start at rest as well.

options.text: Their momenta add together, giving twice the momentum that one skater has on its own
options.rationale: Momenta are added as plain numbers, so the opposite directions do not cancel as they should.

mcqs.stem: A moving trolley collides with a stationary trolley and slows down, while the second trolley moves off. Which description is correct?

options.text: Some momentum was destroyed in the collision, which is why the first trolley slowed down
options.rationale: Momentum appears to vanish when an object slows, but here it has been transferred, not lost.

options.text: Each trolley keeps the momentum it began with, since momentum is a conserved quantity
options.rationale: 'Conserved' is applied to each object separately instead of to the total for the system.

options.text: The momentum lost by the first trolley equals the momentum gained by the second, so the total is unchanged
options.rationale: In a closed system the total momentum before the event equals the total momentum after it.

options.text: The second trolley gains momentum but the first loses more, so the total falls in the collision
options.rationale: Recognises the transfer but assumes some is used up; in a closed system the two changes are equal.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?

options.rationale: Momentum before = 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s. Afterwards the moving mass is 5 kg, so v = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

options.text: 4 m/s
options.rationale: Divides the 12 kg m/s by 3 kg, the first trolley alone, so the trolleys appear to carry on unchanged.

options.text: 12 kg m/s
options.rationale: The total momentum given as the answer, with the final division by the moving mass left out.
The mass divided by the momentum, so the rearrangement has been made upside down.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg ball. The first ball stops. What is the velocity of the second ball?

options.text: 8 m/s
options.rationale: Assumes the second ball takes the velocity of the first rather than its momentum.

options.text: 12 m/s
options.rationale: Found by multiplying 8 by 1.5 instead of dividing the momentum by the mass.

options.text: 4 kg m/s
options.rationale: The momentum of the system, 4 kg m/s, given as if it were the velocity.
Momentum before = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m/s. All of it passes to the 1.5 kg ball, so v = 4 / 1.5 = 2.7 m/s.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A 50 kg skater at rest pushes a 15 kg sledge away at 4 m/s. What is the skater's velocity after the push?

options.text: 4 m/s backwards
options.rationale: Assumes the two objects move apart at the same speed, which would not keep the total at zero.

options.text: 1.2 m/s backwards
options.rationale: The total momentum stays zero, so 50 × v = 15 × 4 = 60, giving v = 1.2 m/s in the opposite direction.

options.text: 13.3 m/s backwards
options.rationale: Uses the mass ratio the wrong way round; the heavier skater must move more slowly, not faster.

options.text: 60 kg m/s backwards
options.rationale: The momentum of the sledge quoted as the skater's velocity, with the division by 50 kg missing.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A resultant force acts on an object that is free to move. What does the specification say happens?

options.text: The object's momentum is transferred into the force, which is why the object slows down again
options.rationale: Treats force as an object that can hold momentum rather than as the cause of the change.

options.text: The mass of the object changes, since momentum is mass × velocity and the momentum changes
options.rationale: Mass is fixed; it is the velocity term in p = m v that the force changes.

options.text: The object's velocity changes but its momentum does not, because its mass is unchanged
options.rationale: Treats momentum as a property of the mass alone, so a change of velocity is thought not to matter.

options.text: A change in momentum occurs, because the force changes the object's velocity in that time
options.rationale: 4.5.7.3 states that when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?

options.text: F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
options.rationale: These are the two equations named in 4.5.7.3; substituting the second into the first gives the momentum form.

options.text: p = m v and a = (v - u)/(t)
options.rationale: The acceleration equation is right, but momentum is the result of the combination, not an input to it.

options.text: F = m × a and a = ∆v × ∆t
options.rationale: Reads acceleration as a product of change in velocity and time, which would put ∆t on the top of the final equation.

options.text: F = m × a and E = ½ m v²
options.rationale: Brings in kinetic energy, which contains no time, so ∆t could not appear in the result.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) Which statement describes the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) correctly?

options.text: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, multiplied by the time over which it changes
options.rationale: Reads the fraction as a product, which would make a slow change produce the larger force.

options.text: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, divided by the time taken for that change
options.rationale: m ∆ v is the change in momentum, so the equation says force equals the rate of change of momentum.

options.text: The force equals the time taken divided by the change in momentum that occurs during it
options.rationale: The fraction inverted, so the units come out as seconds per kilogram metre per second.

options.text: The force equals the momentum of the object divided by the time it has been moving for
options.rationale: Uses the momentum itself rather than the change in it, so a steadily moving object would need a force.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆ v represent?

options.text: The average momentum of the object during the time ∆t while the force is acting on it
options.rationale: Uses the momentum rather than the change in it; ∆ marks a change, not an average.

options.text: The change in momentum, that is the mass multiplied by the change in velocity
options.rationale: The specification states directly that m ∆ v = change in momentum.

options.text: The total momentum the object had before the force began to act on it, in kg m/s
options.rationale: Reads m ∆ v as the starting momentum, so no subtraction is made.

options.text: The change in the force acting, which is the mass multiplied by the change in acceleration
options.rationale: Substitutes force for momentum, the same confusion that turns p = m v into p = m a.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) The specification says force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of' add?

options.text: Nothing of substance; the force is simply equal to the change in momentum that takes place
options.rationale: Drops the 'rate of' part, so two crashes with very different stopping times would give equal forces.

options.text: That the momentum is multiplied by the time for which the resultant force acts on the object
options.rationale: Turns the division into a multiplication, which would make slow changes the most forceful ones.

options.text: That the change in momentum is divided by the time taken for that change to happen
options.rationale: 'Rate of' means per second, which is why ∆t appears on the bottom of F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

options.text: That the momentum changes at a steady rate whenever any resultant force acts on an object
options.rationale: Describes a special case rather than what the phrase 'rate of' means in the statement.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) Why does an air bag reduce the force on a passenger during a crash?

options.text: It reduces the passenger's change in momentum, so there is less momentum to be got rid of
options.rationale: The change in momentum is set by the mass and the change in velocity; the bag cannot alter it.

options.text: It absorbs most of the force of the crash, so that only a little of it reaches the passenger
options.rationale: 'Absorbing the impact' is an everyday phrase; force is not a substance that can be soaked up.

options.text: It brings the passenger to rest more quickly, before they can strike anything solid nearby
options.rationale: A shorter time would raise the rate of change of momentum and so increase the force.

options.text: It increases the time taken for the change in momentum, lowering the rate of change
options.rationale: The same change in momentum spread over a longer time gives a smaller force, from F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A gymnast lands on a crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Why is the force on the gymnast smaller?

options.text: The mat soaks up much of the force of the landing, so that only a small share of it reaches the gymnast
options.rationale: Force is imagined as a substance that can be absorbed, rather than as a rate of change of momentum.

options.text: The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum before the landing, so there is less momentum to be removed
options.rationale: The momentum on reaching the mat is fixed by the fall; the mat changes the time, not the momentum.

options.text: The mat lowers the gymnast's mass on impact, so the change in momentum m ∆ v is made smaller
options.rationale: Mass does not change on landing; only the stopping time is different.

options.text: The mat squashes, so the momentum falls to zero over a longer time, making F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) less
options.rationale: The change in momentum is the same either way; the mat increases ∆t, which reduces the force.

mcqs.stem: (physics only) A 70 kg passenger moving at 12 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s without an air bag, and in 0.6 s with one. What are the two forces?

options.text: 84 N and 504 N
options.rationale: The change in momentum multiplied by the time instead of divided by it, so the bag appears to raise the force.

options.text: 8400 N and 504 N
options.rationale: The first force is right, but the second multiplies the change in momentum by 0.6 instead of dividing.

options.text: 840 N and 840 N
options.rationale: The change in momentum quoted as the force, so the stopping time makes no difference.
